title: American Missionary Kevin Rideout Released After 9 Months' Captivity Following Niamey Kidnapping
detail: Kevin Rideout, a 50-year-old American missionary pilot with SIM International who had worked in Niger for 19 years, was released to US officials on August 14, 2026, nearly 10 months after being abducted by three armed men outside his home in Niamey — about 100 yards from the presidential palace — on October 21, 2025. His abductors headed toward Niger's western Tillabéri region, where he was believed at times to have been held across the border in Mali by the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISGS), though it was unclear which group held him at the end of his captivity, as he may have been moved. No armed group publicly claimed responsibility for the kidnapping, and details of the negotiations and manner of release were not disclosed. SIM International said Rideout is 'in good health in the care of US officials' and would soon be reunited with his family; a US official told CNN he is in FBI custody. President Trump announced the release on Truth Social, saying Rideout had been 'kidnapped by Jihadi terrorists.'

title: UN Report: $50 Million UAE-Linked Hostage Ransom Helped Fund JNIM's 2026 Mali Offensive
detail: A UN sanctions monitoring report, cited by Reuters on August 14, 2026, found that most of an estimated $50 million ransom paid in 2025 for the release of a hostage was redistributed among JNIM katibas operating across the Sahel, with three regional sources identifying the United Arab Emirates as the country that made the payment (a UAE official did not confirm specifics). The report said a portion of the funds went to Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) — JNIM's official al-Qaeda affiliate — which passed some proceeds to al-Qaeda's core leadership and to al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen. The UN experts said the funds 'played a key role in financing the group's offensive across Mali,' referring to JNIM's 2026 campaign including the April 25 coordinated attacks and the ongoing Bamako blockade. The report estimated JNIM's total strength in the Sahel at 7,000–8,000 fighters, roughly half based in Mali. The hostage's identity was not disclosed in the report.

title: FLA Frees 82 Malian Soldiers Held Since April Attacks in Algeria-Mediated Release
detail: Mali's army announced on August 14, 2026 that 82 soldiers held captive by armed groups since the April 25 nationwide attacks had been freed, in a release mediated by Algeria. The Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said it had released 'about 80' Malian soldiers captured between 2023 and 2026, describing the move as 'strictly humanitarian' via spokesperson Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane; Mali's army called it the result of 'rigorous planning and coordinated mobilization.' Mali's Ministry of Foreign Affairs credited Algerian mediation. The FLA said roughly 118 additional Malian soldiers remain in its custody. The release follows the April 25 JNIM-FLA coordinated offensive that hit Bamako's airport, Kati, and other sites and killed Mali's defense minister.
